title: The sounds of Walden
hookLine: the train whistle, the owl, the bullfrogs: Walden's sounds (Walden 4)
last: SOME MORNINGS ARE TOO PRECIOUS TO TRADE FOR WORK.

cards: A scream across the treetops, like a hawk over a farmyard. Then a rumble, and the railroad cars roll past the far edge of the pond. Later, church bells from distant towns, softened by miles of woods.
At dusk, a whip-poor-will. At night, owls. And from the water's edge, a deep, absurd croaking that carries on into the night.
It's easy to assume Thoreau went to the woods for silence. But the chapter right after Reading is called Sounds, and it's full of noise.

teach.b: First, a second kind of reading. Sounds begins by turning from books. If you read only written languages, Thoreau warns, you may forget "the language which all things and events speak without metaphor."
The world is also a text, and listening is how you read it.

teach.h: THE TRAIN IS PART OF IT.
teach.b: Second, the train. He doesn't pretend the railroad isn't there.
The whistle cuts through his woods summer and winter, and he's half annoyed, half thrilled. He watches the cars carry goods from far away, and notices townspeople setting their clocks by them.
The modern world is part of the soundscape, and he listens to it too. Third, the bells and the birds. On some Sundays he could hear church bells from several towns.
Crossing the woods, the sound changed, as if the pine needles on the horizon were the strings of a harp and the bell had swept across them. The distance made its own music.
Then the evening birds: whip-poor-wills, and owls whose cries he calls mournful and strange, and which he's glad are there. Fourth, the frogs.
Late at night, the bullfrogs take over the pond, trumping to each other across the water.
Thoreau writes their croak down as a long, rolling sound, and clearly enjoys them. Nothing here is holy in the usual sense. That's the point.
Close attention turns a train, an owl and a frog into a kind of reading.

how: Some readers of Walden practice sitting still outdoors and naming what they hear, after the Sounds chapter, including the noises of roads and trains as well as birds.

games.q: what does “the sounds of walden” mean?
o: Thoreau's chapter of listening to trains, bells and frogs
Thoreau's praise of the total silence of the woods
a book of hymns once sung in Concord's churches

games.q: inside the sounds of Walden: tap the pairs.
p: like a hawk's scream over a farm
swept across the pines like a harp
trumping across the pond at night

s: at Walden, Thoreau heard only nature
the railroad ran past the pond, and its whistle reached his woods summer and winter.
the Sounds chapter begins by turning from books to listening
he warns that reading only written languages can make us forget the language all things speak.
Thoreau found the owls' cries unbearable
he describes them as mournful and strange, and says he is glad there are owls.

games.q: you've moved to the woods for quiet, and a train whistle screams through the trees. what does Thoreau do with it?
o: complain and try to block it out.
listen to it too, as part of the place.
games.why: he writes about the train at length, half annoyed and half thrilled, as one of the sounds of Walden.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen the way Thoreau listened from his doorway: find one sound and name it plainly, a fan, a car, a bird, your own breath, then a second, until you have five.
Some will be near and some far, some pleasant and some not. Don't sort them into good and bad; let each one be part of the place you're in.

wordCard.voice: The sounds of Walden. Thoreau's chapter of listening: the train whistle, distant bells, owls, bullfrogs, and what he calls the language all things and events speak without metaphor. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sounds. Even the one you'd tune out is part of the reading. Same time tomorrow.
